newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Cyprus dispute threatens EU/NATO enlargement.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus dispute threatens EU/NATO enlargement.

text.p: European Union countries expressed alarm on Monday that the tense stand-off between Greece and Turkey in the southern Mediterranean could knock off course plans for both NATO and EU enlargement.

Diplomats said Ankara, angered by what it sees as a pro-Greece bias by the West, was increasingly hinting it would block plans to expand the alliance into former communist Europe unless the EU delivered on promises of closer ties.

As a member of NATO, Turkey can veto new applicants and also block plans to lend the Western European Union (WEU), the EU's nascent defence wing, NATO equipment to allow the Europeans to develop a separate security identity.
"The Turks are threatening to do in NATO what the Greeks do in the European Union, the whole thing could become very messy," said one European diplomat.

The West has struggled to keep NATO and EU politics apart, but Turkish diplomats started to link the two after Greece succeeded in blocking funds for Ankara expected to flow under a historic customs pact signed with the EU in 1996.

The economic pact was presented as a precursor to possible full membership, a recognition of Turkey's vital strategic importance on the EU's fragile southern flank, and a means of checking the growth of radical Islam.

The EU's failure to deliver the economic benefits foreseen under the deal has weakened the pro-western, secularist parties who joined the country's first Islamist-led coalition after losing elections last year to the main Moslem party.

The prospect of the two enlargements, already highly complex, becoming entangled has left western capitals fearing a dangerous diplomatic gridlock which could weaken its hand in critical talks with Russia.
"We do not think it is appropriate to use one (enlargement) to affect the other," British Minister of State David Davis told reporters.

NATO has told Russia alliance enlargement will go ahead and new members will be named next July at a special summit in Madrid, hoping Moscow can now be encouraged to sign a new pact with the West accepting it as a reality.

Sniping between Athens and Ankara -- exacerbated by failure to make any progress towards resolving the issue of Cyprus -- could also further complicate plans to begin the next stage of enlarging the European Union.

German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Monday that Cyprus -- divided into Greek-Cypriot and Turkish-Cypriot zones since 1974 -- could not become a member until the long-standing dispute was settled.
"Anyone who wants to join the EU must know that the European Union cannot deal with the accession of new members that bring in additional external problems," he told reporters.
The EU has said it will open accession talks with Cyprus some six months after the end of this year's internal review of its treaties.
Central and eastern European countries are pushing for the same commitment and fear a failure to solve the Cyprus question could delay the start of talks with other applicant nations.

Privately, several EU diplomats sympathise with Turkey and are furious with Greece for not exerting more pressure on the Greek-Cypriot government in Nicosia to drop its plan to deploy air defence missiles on the divided island.
Turkey immediately said it would use force to stop the deployment of the missiles, triggering a frantic bout of U.S. diplomacy to head off another potential clash in the Aegean.
